title: TLS/SSL
subtitle: The TLS handshake, cipher suites, forward secrecy, and HTTPS

whyItExists.problem: HTTP sends all data in plaintext. Any network device between client and server (ISP, router, café Wi-Fi) can read passwords, cookies, and credit card numbers.
whyItExists.solution: TLS (Transport Layer Security) wraps the connection: the client and server negotiate keys, authenticate the server via its certificate, and all data is encrypted with AES-GCM. The whole handshake takes under 1ms with TLS 1.3.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Every web application, API, database connection, and email server. TLS is the foundation of HTTPS. Never deploy without it.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Internal loopback connections (localhost) where there is no network path for interception. Even then, consider TLS for consistency.

explainModes.beginner: TLS is what puts the 'S' in HTTPS. It creates a secure tunnel between your browser and the website so nobody in the middle can read your data or pretend to be the website.
explainModes.simple: TLS has two phases: a handshake where both sides agree on encryption keys and verify the server's identity using a certificate, then a data phase where all communication is encrypted with AES.
explainModes.standard: TLS 1.3 handshake: Client Hello (key share + cipher list), Server Hello (key share + certificate), Both sides derive symmetric keys from ECDH, all subsequent traffic uses AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305.
explainModes.technical: TLS 1.3 reduces handshake to 1 RTT (or 0-RTT for resumption). Key exchange uses ECDHE for forward secrecy. The server's certificate is signed by a CA. Session keys are derived using HKDF from the ECDH shared secret. TLS 1.0/1.1 are deprecated (RFC 8996).
explainModes.deepDive: TLS 1.3 eliminated all weak cipher suites (RC4, 3DES, DES, CBC-based), required forward secrecy (no RSA key exchange), and removed renegotiation. 0-RTT resumption allows replaying data but is vulnerable to replay attacks, so it must only be used for idempotent requests. Certificate Transparency logs (CT) are required for all certificates since 2018.

content.text: TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts data in transit between client and server. It provides confidentiality (eavesdropping prevention), integrity (tampering detection), and authentication (server identity verification). TLS 1.3 is the current version — TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated and must not be used.

content.code:
TLS 1.3 Handshake (1 round-trip)

Client → Server: ClientHello
  - Supported cipher suites: TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256
  - Key share: X25519 public key (for ECDHE)
  - Random nonce

Server → Client: ServerHello + Certificate + CertificateVerify + Finished
  - Chosen cipher suite
  - Key share: X25519 public key
  - Certificate (signed by CA) → proves server identity
  - CertificateVerify: signature over handshake using private key
  - Finished: HMAC over entire handshake (tamper detection)

Both sides:
  - Compute ECDHE shared secret from key shares
  - Derive session keys using HKDF
  - All further data encrypted with AES-256-GCM

Total: 1 round-trip before data flows

content.text: Forward secrecy is a critical TLS 1.3 feature. Each connection uses fresh ECDHE key pairs that are discarded after the session. Even if the server's private key is later compromised, past sessions cannot be decrypted because the session keys were derived from ephemeral keys that no longer exist.

content.definition: Property that ensures past sessions cannot be decrypted even if long-term keys are later compromised. Achieved in TLS 1.3 by using ephemeral ECDHE for key exchange.
A named combination of algorithms for key exchange, authentication, encryption, and MAC. TLS 1.3 only permits 5 suites, all using AEAD and ephemeral key exchange.

content.code:
import ssl
import socket

# --- TLS Server ---
context = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER)
context.minimum_version = ssl.TLSVersion.TLSv1_2   # enforce TLS 1.2 minimum
context.load_cert_chain("cert.pem", "key.pem")     # certificate + private key

with socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM) as sock:
    sock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    sock.bind(("0.0.0.0", 4443))
    sock.listen(5)
    with context.wrap_socket(sock, server_side=True) as ssock:
        while True:
            conn, addr = ssock.accept()
            with conn:
                data = conn.recv(4096)
                conn.send(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n\r\nHello over TLS!")

# --- TLS Client (verify certificate) ---
client_context = ssl.create_default_context()   # loads system trust store
with socket.create_connection(("example.com", 443)) as raw:
    with client_context.wrap_socket(raw, server_hostname="example.com") as tls:
        tls.send(b"GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: example.com\r\n\r\n")
        print(tls.recv(4096))

# Check a server's TLS configuration
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -tls1_3 2>/dev/null | head -20

# See which protocols and cipher suites are supported
nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 example.com

# Test with curl (shows TLS version used)
curl -v https://example.com 2>&1 | grep -E 'TLS|SSL|cipher'

# Check certificate expiry
echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -dates

a.name: TLS 1.2
a.description: 2008 standard; widely supported; more flexible but weaker defaults
weaknesses: RSA key exchange allowed (no forward secrecy)
a.useWhen: Only when legacy clients require it; still acceptable with strong cipher suite configuration

b.name: TLS 1.3
b.description: 2018 standard; faster, more secure, forward secrecy required
weaknesses: Older clients (pre-2018) may not support it
b.useWhen: All new deployments — the default choice

content.text: Never disable TLS certificate verification in production (verify=False in requests, ssl.CERT_NONE). It makes the connection vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. If you need to test with self-signed certificates, add the CA certificate to the trust store instead.
Use HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) to tell browsers to always use HTTPS: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains. This prevents protocol-downgrade attacks.

questions.question: What does TLS protect against on a public Wi-Fi network?
options: Eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle interception of data in transit
XSS attacks injected by the server
questions.explanation: TLS encrypts and authenticates data in transit, preventing network-level eavesdroppers from reading or modifying the communication.

questions.question: What is forward secrecy in TLS?
options: The ability to decrypt future sessions without a certificate
Past sessions remain secure even if the server's long-term private key is later compromised
The ability to predict which cipher suite will be used
A technique for reducing handshake latency
questions.explanation: Forward secrecy (PFS) uses ephemeral ECDHE keys discarded after each session. Even if the server's certificate private key leaks, past sessions cannot be decrypted.

questions.question: Which of these is a TLS 1.3 improvement over TLS 1.2?
options: TLS 1.3 supports RC4 for faster encryption
TLS 1.3 reduces the handshake to 1 round-trip and requires forward secrecy
TLS 1.3 uses RSA exclusively for key exchange
TLS 1.3 allows CBC cipher suites for compatibility
questions.explanation: TLS 1.3 reduces the handshake from 2 RTT to 1 RTT, eliminates all weak cipher suites, and mandates forward secrecy via ECDHE.

faq.a: HTTP Strict Transport Security — a response header that tells browsers to only connect via HTTPS for a specified duration (max-age). It prevents protocol downgrade attacks where an attacker tries to redirect HTTPS traffic to HTTP.

faq.q: What is a man-in-the-middle (MitM) attack on TLS?
faq.a: An attacker intercepts the connection and presents their own certificate instead of the real server's. TLS prevents this because the attacker cannot create a valid certificate signed by a trusted CA for a domain they don't control — unless they compromise a CA.

Yes. TLS 1.0 is vulnerable to BEAST and POODLE attacks. TLS 1.1 is marginally better. Both are deprecated by RFC 8996 (2021) and browsers have removed support. Configure your server to require TLS 1.2 as the minimum.

examples: Every HTTPS request uses TLS — the padlock in your browser confirms the certificate is valid and the connection is encrypted
The 2014 Heartbleed bug in OpenSSL let attackers read server memory including private keys from TLS servers
TLS 1.3 deployment grew from 0% to 90%+ of connections between 2018 and 2022
